It is obvious that there can be no oath where, if the defendant admitted liability, he would be exempt as one who admits a fine. Rather, Tosafot's first answer must understand the Mishnah's general formulation to include even a mu'ad ox. In that case the rule that one who cannot swear must pay does apply, and there is no concept of heilech because payment from a mu'ad is taken from superior assets rather than from the body of the ox. In Tosafot's second answer, which establishes the case as one involving a tam, there is no need to invoke heilech because there is no oath at all, since an admission to the fine would exempt him. Moreover, according to one establishment in Shevuot, Shmuel holds that where one claims wheat and barley and the defendant admits one of them, he is exempt from an oath, while heilech itself creates liability according to Rabbenu Tam, as Tosafot write in Bava Metzia 5, s.v. i nami. Yet Shmuel himself is the one who says that the rule applies even where the injured party makes a definite claim, etc. Tosafot therefore needed an answer to Shmuel's statement that works according to every establishment. They could not rely on heilech, since according to Shmuel heilech may obligate rather than exempt. There is thus no proof from that passage. Here, however, the sugya does indicate that Tosafot's answer depends upon treating the tam ox as heilech. There remains a difficulty regarding the middle and final clauses. In the final clause, where the claimant says the larger mu'ad ox caused the damage and the defendant says the smaller mu'ad did, even if we disagree with the Nimukei Yosef, it is impossible to say that the Mishnah follows Rabban Gamliel unless we say that an oath is required, because there is no heilech with respect to a mu'ad. We must therefore say that Tosafot agree with the Nimukei Yosef that this is an admission of the same kind as the claim. If so, the final clause independently must involve one party being uncertain. Yet Rav Pappa does not derive his argument from that clause. This shows that parallelism to the final clause is not essential. Tosafot's question is therefore sound: perhaps the Mishnah follows Rabban Gamliel, while the middle clause involves heilech. In that case, however, what room is there for the Rosh's question against the Rif, who does not accept the Nimukei Yosef's view, as I will explain below in siman 400, and Rambam likewise does not accept it? According to the Rif, full parallelism throughout the Mishnah can indeed be required, and the objection disappears. There is another possible resolution. Rav Pappa does not establish the middle clause as involving seizure because it is certainly strained to interpret a Mishnah that says only that the claimant must bring proof as secretly referring to property already seized by the claimant. Seizure is not mentioned at all. But if, independently, we must say that even though the Mishnah says that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant it nevertheless concerns a case where the injured party had seized the ox, then it is reasonable to say that the seizure occurred from the outset before the claims were made. Once we already know that the Mishnah deals with seizure, we can use that fact throughout. This is relevant according to the view that half damages are a fine. The Rosh asks how the Mishnah can involve the owner's admission, since even if he admitted every detail he would be exempt as one who admits a fine. The Rosh's answer, that there were witnesses but they did not know which ox gored, is strained, like the Gemara's question in Bava Batra: if there are witnesses, let us see what they say. Here too, the difficulty is obvious. The Maggid Mishneh therefore explains that the injured party had seized the ox. Seizure prevents the tortfeasor's admission from exempting him from half damages even according to the view that half damages are a fine. Once the Mishnah must in any event be understood as involving seizure, it is reasonable to say that the injured party seized before making his claim, and then the rule of claiming wheat and admitting barley does not apply. Accordingly, the Rif may hold that the anonymous Gemara, which follows the ruling that half damages are a fine, answers with seizure, and that answer in truth applies to the middle clause as well. The Gemara does not ask from the middle clause because it could have answered that the injured party is fit to take there and has nothing, since no baraita was cited to contradict such an explanation, as I wrote above. But in substance the seizure answer can apply there too. Rav Pappa, by contrast, holds that half damages are compensatory and therefore has no independent reason to introduce seizure into the Mishnah. For him, seizure remains unmentioned and strained, so he cannot use that answer. He therefore establishes the middle clause as one where the injured party is uncertain. The same applies to the final clause. The Rif need not accept Rashi and Tosafot's claim that the clauses would then be redundant, because many distinctions make each clause necessary, as Tosafot themselves discuss. The anonymous Gemara that answers with seizure follows Rabbah bar Mamal and, as explained, can maintain that Sumchus applies even to two definite claims. The entire Mishnah can therefore remain a case of two definite claims. Everything is properly explained.

And there is a clear proof for the Rif that the seizure explanation applies to the first clause as well. We must explain Rav Pappa's establishment of the middle clause as one where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, and the first clause in the reverse, with the injured party certain and the tortfeasor uncertain. Although the Mishnah says "No, rather," which ordinarily indicates two definite claims, Tosafot and Maharsha explain that the clause includes such a case but that Sumchus's disagreement is relevant only to the case of uncertainty. At first glance, why was Rav Pappa forced to make the first and middle clauses only imperfectly parallel, with uncertainty on opposite sides? It would seem simpler to establish both as cases where both parties are uncertain. In such a case Sumchus and the Sages disagree directly. It is true that the middle clause also includes the case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, which explains the words "No, rather," but there would then be no novelty in saying that Sumchus does not require division in that subcase. One could hardly say that the entire first clause is superfluous, because if it comes merely to teach that Sumchus requires division where both are uncertain, many Mishnayot already establish that rule, such as the beginning of chapter HaParah and the Mishnayot concerning the borrowed and rented animals and concerning an exchange. Nor is it necessary to teach that the Sages disagree even there. If, in the middle clause where there is partial admission, the Sages nevertheless say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, then all the more so in the first clause where the defendant totally denies liability. We must therefore say that the first clause concerns an injured party making a definite claim and a tortfeasor who is uncertain. It teaches that even there the Sages apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, contrary to Sumchus. The middle clause must correspondingly be understood in that way as well to the extent the wording allows, which is strained, as Maharsha notes. Were it not for the implication of "No, rather," we would have established the whole matter as uncertainty on both sides. There is, however, a way to explain the wording. In the first clause, although the main dispute between Sumchus and the Sages concerns the case where the injured party is certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, the Mishnah still says "No, rather" because it also includes two definite claims. It teaches that even where the ox was a mu'ad that was pursuing the injured animal, the Sages nevertheless allow the tortfeasor to say that the animal was struck by a rock, as Rambam rules, contrary to the view of Maharshal. The Mishnah says simply "an ox," which includes a mu'ad. But in the middle clause, if the actual dispute were only where both parties were uncertain, why would the Mishnah say "No, rather" merely to include an additional case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain? There would be no practical dispute in that additional case, since Sumchus too would agree that the possessor's definite claim prevails. The phrase would teach nothing. Therefore the middle clause itself must involve a case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, and even there Sumchus requires division while the Sages apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. If so, the final clause likewise necessarily involves the injured party uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, at least according to Rabbah bar Mamal, who maintains that the first clause involves two definite claims and whose approach still requires the middle clause to have the tortfeasor making a definite claim in order for the wording to be meaningful. But this creates a major difficulty according to Abaye. Tosafot in Bava Batra 135, s.v. Abaye, write that Abaye holds that even where the uncertain party had absolutely no reason to know, a definite claim is still superior. How then can the first clause, where the injured party is certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, conclude according to the Sages that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant? The claimant's definite claim should prevail. All the more so in the middle clause, where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, why should Sumchus require division? Tosafot's answer that the uncertain party had no reason to know does not work according to Abaye. This is a powerful difficulty. The Rif therefore must hold as I have written, that once the Gemara introduces seizure, that answer applies to the middle clause as well and the clauses can be understood as cases of two definite claims. Abaye can explain the middle clause as two definite claims, where Sumchus and the Sages disagree, without any difficulty from the principle that a definite claim is superior to an uncertain one. The rule of seizure also removes the difficulty from Rabbah bar Natan. Thus the Rif's interpretation is necessary for Abaye according to the view attributed to him by Tosafot in Bava Batra. This is, in my opinion, a clear and powerful proof for the Rif. Tosafot in HaManiach, who do not apply seizure to the first and middle clauses, follow their own view in chapter HaParah that even Abaye agrees that where the uncertain party had no reason to know, a definite claim is not superior. They therefore face no difficulty. The Rif, however, follows the other approach recorded by Tosafot in Bava Batra, as explained above, and his position has a clear proof.

The value of the barley. The Sema writes that the reason is that since the claimant is already in possession, he can say, "I neither admitted nor waived the barley. I merely did not wish to demand everything at once." These are his words. At first glance they are incomprehensible. According to the Rama, seizure helps specifically if it occurred before the admission, but not afterward. If the Sema's reasoning were correct, seizure afterward should also help, because the claimant could say, "I know that I did not waive it." One cannot answer that this would be seizure after the doubt arose, because where the possessor makes a definite claim, seizure is effective even after the doubt arose, as the Rosh writes in Ketubot and Bava Metzia. See what I wrote above in the rules of seizure. This is particularly so according to the Mechaber, who holds that seizure even after the doubt arises is effective. We must therefore say that the Sema's reason was written only according to the opinion that seizure is effective even afterward, not according to those who distinguish based on the timing of seizure. Yet the Sema himself, in seif katan 26, cites the Nimukei Yosef's view distinguishing between seizure before the claimant's retraction and seizure afterward. His words therefore remain difficult. The Tur explicitly gives a different reason. He writes: since the claimant seized the barley, his failure to demand it is not considered an admission, because he can say, "I did not demand the barley because I was already in possession of it." This is a different explanation from the Sema's. Still, even the Rosh requires explanation. According to his own view, seizure helps only in the case of the two oxen. He writes: therefore, if the injured party seized before coming to beit din, even in the presence of witnesses, he collects according to what the tortfeasor says. Why does the Rosh require seizure specifically before coming to beit din? In the case of the two injured animals, the explanation that "I did not demand the smaller one because I was already in possession of it" seems inapplicable. The injured party cannot truthfully mean to demand both the large and the small ox, because the two claims are mutually exclusive. If the larger ox caused the damage, the smaller did not. Once he asserts in beit din that the larger ox caused the damage, he can no longer say that the smaller ox did. One might answer that this reason is needed only where the claimant could have claims regarding both items, whereas where the claims are mutually exclusive no such reason is necessary. But if so, the Rosh's objection to the Rif would fail. With wheat and barley it is possible that both claims are true, whereas with one large and one small ox both claims cannot be true. What then does seizure help there, since the Tur's explanation cannot apply? It is strained to say that the injured party could have come to beit din and said explicitly, "In my view the larger ox caused the damage, but if it is established otherwise, or if the owner admits only the smaller ox, then at least give me the value of the smaller." Such a formulation indeed would avoid both admission and waiver. If the claimant had seized, it could be treated as though he had made that reservation, because according to the Rosh both oxen are in his hands, while according to the Rif at least the smaller one is in his hands. This also resolves another difficulty in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. They state generally that seizure helps. That is understandable if, according to the claimant, there were two separate loans, one of wheat and one of barley, even if they occurred on the same day and at the same hour. But what if, according to both parties, there was only one loan, and they disagree whether it was wheat or barley? The defendant is exempt, exactly like the case of one large and one small ox. In such a case seizure should seemingly not help even according to the Rif. The claimant cannot say, "Because I had already seized the barley I did not demand it," for he did demand this very loan and admitted by his formulation that it was not barley. According to what I have written, however, the matter is resolved. Seizure is treated as though the claimant had expressly reserved his rights by saying, "I am certain it was wheat, but if in fact it was barley, I do not waive or admit away that claim." Such a reservation works in every case. Yet even if we can interpret the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in this way according to the Rif, it is difficult to explain the Rosh this way because he grounds the rule in the claimant's admission. What reservation can overcome an express admission that the smaller ox did not damage the larger animal? Unless we say that the ultimate effect of such an admission is waiver, so that seizure is treated as though the claimant expressly stipulated that he does not waive. This itself is proof against the Shach's explanation of the Rosh above. All of this is strained if we distinguish between situations where the claimant could have claims against both items and situations where he could not. The same reasoning should apply even where the claims are mutually exclusive. There is also a difficulty in Tosafot. At the beginning of chapter HaParah, Tosafot ask according to Rashbam's view that Sumchus did not state his division rule where both parties make definite claims except when the disputed property stands in a neutral place, whereas when it is in the possessor's house Sumchus agrees that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. If so, why did Rabbah bar Mamal feel compelled to say that the Mishnah does not follow Sumchus? Let the Mishnah follow Sumchus and concern a case where the tortfeasor's ox remained in the tortfeasor's house, in which case Sumchus agrees that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. Yam Shel Shlomo discusses this question at length and treats it as a strong argument against Rashbam. But how can the Mishnah be explained that way? In the final clause involving the two injured animals, the difficulty from Rabbah bar Natan's rule of claiming wheat and admitting barley would remain. We would then have to say that the injured party seized both oxen, as the Rosh writes, and that the seizure occurred before he came to beit din. But if the ox is in the injured party's house, that is stronger possession than if it stood in a neutral field. Surely his position should not become weaker merely because he brought it into his own house. According to Sumchus, the Mishnah should therefore require division rather than simply apply the burden of proof to the claimant. The result could not be that the injured party either takes according to the tortfeasor or takes nothing where he did not seize, while if he did seize they divide. How then can the Mishnah simply state that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, implying that with proof he takes according to the tortfeasor's admission? It follows that the Mishnah cannot follow Sumchus and must follow the Sages. According to the Sages, the Mishnah must be teaching their rule specifically against Sumchus, and therefore we establish the case as one where the ox stands in a neutral place, where Sumchus would require division. This entirely resolves Tosafot's question. Why, then, would Tosafot force any strained answer that undermines Rashbam when such a straightforward answer is available? This suggests at first glance that Tosafot do not hold that seizure must occur before the parties stand in beit din. Perhaps seizure afterward also helps. Then one can say that at the time of judgment the tortfeasor's ox was in the tortfeasor's house, and only afterward did the injured party seize it. Sumchus could then agree at the first stage that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, while the later seizure addresses Rabbah bar Natan's rule. Yet we find no authority who explicitly disagrees regarding the requirement that seizure precede the litigation. In particular, the Rosh states the requirement without qualification, and Tosafot ordinarily would not disagree with him without the Rosh mentioning their position. It therefore appears that the Rosh holds as follows. Even if the claimant later says, "I did not intend to admit anything," we disregard that subjective intention because unexpressed thoughts have no legal effect. Rather, beit din itself is uncertain whether the claimant's original formulation constitutes a complete admission that exempts the defendant from the barley or whether it does not. Because this is only a slight doubt and the language leans toward admission and waiver, the claimant must satisfy two conditions in order for seizure to prevail. First, he must have seized before the doubt arose in beit din, meaning before he made the relevant claim there. Second, the seizure must have been lawful, as the Rosh writes in Bechorot in the name of Ramban, that seizure must be with permission. That means that the possessor must have had a right to seize the very item based on the claim he was asserting, as Terumat HaDeshen explains. I discussed this principle at length above in the treatise on seizure. Therefore, the claimant must have some legitimate claim concerning both items, so that his seizure is lawful. Where, according to his own position, he has no claim at all to one of the items, seizure of that item was not lawful and is ineffective. This resolves the issue. Accordingly, Tosafot can also be understood. Since beit din itself is uncertain whether the claimant's words amounted to admission and waiver, Sumchus would require division because Sumchus applies his division rule to a doubt that exists for beit din, just as in the case of whether an intercalated month belongs to the renter or the owner, where the doubt is whether we follow the first expression or the last. The authorities write that the opinion requiring division there is Sumchus. See what I wrote above in the rules of seizure. If so, were the Mishnah according to Sumchus, as Tosafot ask, there would be no need to assume seizure at all. The difficulty from the baraita that says that without proof he takes according to the tortfeasor would disappear because in truth, according to Sumchus, he would not simply take according to the tortfeasor. He would take half of the amount admitted by the tortfeasor, since beit din is uncertain whether the claimant's earlier words constituted admission or waiver, and Sumchus requires division in such a doubt. The Mishnah could not simply say "exempt," because the claimant would collect half of what the tortfeasor admitted. One might object that if the disputed ox is in the tortfeasor's house, Sumchus does not require division. That is true only where the possessor makes a definite claim. Where the possessor himself is uncertain, Sumchus requires division even when the property is in his house, as Tosafot explicitly write in Bava Metzia 100 based on the Mishnah concerning the borrowed and rented animals. Here the tortfeasor cannot make a definite legal claim that the claimant's language constituted admission. The legal effect of that language is itself uncertain. Therefore Sumchus would always require division. Everything is properly explained. This approach, however, cannot explain the Rif and Rambam according to the Mechaber, who holds that seizure even after the doubt arose is effective. According to them, we must instead use the Tur's reason, namely that since the claimant had seized the barley, his failure to demand it does not constitute an admission. Where even the claimant agrees that there was only one loan, we must resort to the more strained explanation above, that seizure is treated as though he expressly stipulated that even if the loan is found to have been barley, he neither waives nor admits away his right. This matter still requires study.

he_segments: דשטר הוי כמו קרקע דעת הסמ"ע כמ"ש באריכות בדרישה דאפילו לא היה לו ולא אית ליה קרקע כלל מ"מ הוי שעבוד קרקעות הואיל ונזכר בי' ש"ק. ונמשך אחריו הרב בט"ז וראי' מהא דכתב הטור בשם התו' והרא"ש דלמ"ד שעבודא דאורייתא לא משכחן שבועה דאוריית' במ"מ וכדומה אלא בדלית ליה קרקע וא"כ עכצ"ל דשטר הוי ש"ק אפי' בדלית ליה קרקע דאי אית ליה אפילו מלוה על פה וכת"י נמי יהיה ש"ק אלא דשטר חשוב ש"ק אפילו לית ליה קרקע. והש"ך חולק וכ"נ דעת הב"ח דבאין לו קרקע אף שטר אין לו שעבוד ולא מיקרי ש"ק והא דקרא לשטר ש"ק ומחלק בין שטר לכת"י בדמחל על ב"ח ולא מחל על משעבדי ולכך איקרי שטר ש"ק ולא מלוה ע"פ וכת"י. ואמת דהך סברא כתבו התו' בריש ב"מ בשמעתי' דהילך אבל קשה לכוונו בלשון הטור דלא ה"ל לסתום בשטר דהוי ש"ק רק לפר' באופן שכתב הש"ך דמחל ע"ז ולא ע"ז ועוד הטור כתב דברי רמב"ן דבאבד השטר או א"י לקיימו לא קרוי ש"ק וע"ז כתב הטור אבל התו' והרא"ש כתבו דלא משכחת מ"מ אלא בדלית ליה קרקע וכו' מזה מבואר דס"ל דהם חולקים ארמב"ן ולפי דברי הש"ך אף הרמב"ן יכול לסבור זה רק מיירי בשטר באופן דמיירי ביה הטור לדעת הש"ך דמחל על ב"ח ולא על משעבדי ולכך בדאיתא לשטר גובה ממשעבדי ה"ל ש"ק אבל בדליתא או אינו מקוים דלא גבי מלקוחות לא קרוי ש"ק ואין כאן מחלוקת כלל: ולכן נראה דבדרישה נתקשה בדברי התו' בשבועות דהקשו במימרא דר"י הכופר במלוה שיש לו עדים חייב ק"ש ובשטר פטור משום דה"ל ש"ק והקשו התו' והרא"ש הא ר"י ס"ל ש"ד ואף בעדים הוי ש"ק ותי' התו' דל"ל קדקע או דמחיל ליה ועדיי' הקושיא במקומו כמו שבאמת התו' בב"מ הרגישו בו א"כ אף במלוה בשטר נמי ובב"מ תי' כמ"ש הש"ך דמחל על ב"ח ולא על משעבדי אך בשבועות דלא כתבו קושי' זו ולא תי' זו קשה וכבר תמה בזה מהר"ם מלובלין בחדושיו לב"מ על הך דברי תו' דשבועות והדרישה רצה מכח זה להוכיח דעתו דבשטר אפי' ל"ל קרקע מ"מ ש"ק מיקרי ובאמת יפה כתב הש"ך דדבר זה אין לו שחר אבל התרת קושיא זו נקל דס"ל שם לתו' והרא"ש כמ"ש רוב המחברים דעכשיו דתקנו חכמים מלוה ע"פ אינו גובה משעבדי א"כ אין כאן שעבוד כלל אפי' על ב"ח דהא כל רגע בידו למוכרו מבלי מוחה רק הא דגובה בישנו ביד לוה משום דמיניה אפי' מגלימא וכו' אבל שעבודא ליכא כלל רק קושית התו' על התורה דהתורה כתבה שבועה במ"מ ודכוותיה הא ה"ל ש"ק והיכן משכחת ליה שבועה ועל זה תירץ דאי אתה מוצא ש"ד לדינו של תורה רק בדלית ליה קרקע או מחיל אבל ר' יוחנן אמרו למילתא לדינא בתר דתקנו חז"ל דמלוה ע"פ אין טורף מלקוחות ואפקיעוהו רבנן לשעבודא ולכך אף בדאית ליה קרקע חייב קרבן שבועה בכיפר במלוה שיש לו עדים אבל בשטר לא דבהך קיימא שעבודא ולא הפקיעו חז"ל וא"ש: וזהו נראה ברור דעת הטור ולכך בכל סי' ע"ה וסי' פ"ז דהזכיר דיני ש"ד וההבדל שיש בין ש"ד לשבועה דרבנן לא הזכיר תנאי זה שיהיה דוקא הלוה גברא דלית ליה קרקע או מחל משום דלדינא ליתא דאף באית ליה אפקיעוהו רבנן לשעבודא וזהו במלוה ע"פ או כת"י אבל במלוה בשטר לא נפקע השעבוד וה"ל ש"ק ביש לו קרקע וזהו הבדל שיש בין שטר לבע"פ וכת"י ומה שהביא הטור דברי התו' והרא"ש הוא לכוונה זה דעל הך קושיא דמ"מ איך משכחת ליה תי' הר"ן בשבועות וכמש"ל בסי' ע"ה באריכות דבריו דמה בכך דנכסיו משועבדים מ"מ אם יבא הדבר לטריפת לקוחות הלקוחות יכחשו בו ויאמרו מה נ"מ לנו בהודאתך שקר אתה אומר אין אתה חייב לו לא לוה או נפרע ולכך אינו קרוי ש"ק אף דש"ד ותי' זה ס"ל לרמב"ן נמי כמ"ש הרא"ש בשמו סוף פרק שבועות פקדון ע"ש אבל התוס' וביחוד הרא"ש שם מיאנו בתי' זה דס"ל כיון אלו ידוע דחייב לו הוי ש"ק אף דבאמת דאין יכול לטרוף מלקוחות כי לא יאמינו לו מ"מ גוף הלואה אית ביה ש"ק ולכך לא משכחינן ש"ד ביה וצ"ל דלית ליה קרקע ע"ש והנ"מ בין שני סברות הללו במלוה בשטר דשעבוד של תורה קאי אף לדידן ונאבד השטר רק הלוה מודה בו לדעת הרמב"ן אין כאן ש"ק דהא א"א לטרוף מלקוחות דלא יאמינו לו דהיה לו שטר ונאבד דאולי להד"ם או פרע וא"כ לא הוי מודה בש"ק והודאתו ה"ל ש"ד אבל לדעת התו' והרא"ש דס"ל לדין תורה מ"מ קרוי ש"ק אף דלא יאמינו לו הלקוחות כמ"ש א"כ ה"ה לשטר שנאבד ולוה מודה בו אף דלא יאמינו לקוחות מ"מ גופו של הלואה יש בו ש"ק והוי זה כמו מודה מקצת לדינו של תורה. והן הן דברי הטור דבתר דהביא דעת הרמב"ן בשטר בלתי מקוים או נאבד דלא מיקרי ש"ק וחייב שבועת התורה ועל זה כתב אבל התו' והרא"ש כתבו דמ"מ לא משכחת ליה פי' לדינו של תורה כמ"ש רק בדלית ליה קרקע אבל ביש לו לא אף דלקוחות לא יאמינו לו וא"כ ה"ה בשטר שאין מקוים או נאבד והלוה מודה בו ליכא ש"ד וזה ברור ונכון ועיין הרא"ש ס"פ שבועת הפקדון ותראה להדיא כדברי וכן מבואר ומוכח ברא"ש פ"ב דכתובות דכתב בהוא אומר אלמנה נשאתיך וכתובתך מנה והיא אומרת בתולה וכתובתי מאתים הא דלא הוי ביה שבועה דאורייתא כדין מודה מקצת דהוי ליה שעבוד קרקעות דכתובה שעבוד קרקעות הוי וכו' והביא דברי ירושלמי סלעין דאינון ונמחק מלוה אומר חמש ולוה אמר שלש בן עזאי אומר הואיל והודה מקצת טענה ישבע וחכמים אומרים אין זה הודאה ממין טענה פי' שההודאה בקרקע היא נהי נמי דשטרא לית ביה אלא שנים מ"מ כיון שהודה בשלישי הוה ליה כאלו נכתב שטר והכפירה במטלטלין ופריך והא הכא בהיא אומר בתולה ה"ל הודאה ממין טענה שהרי אין לה שטר והיא אומרת ר' והוא אומר ק' ומשני כ"ע מודים דאית לה מנה פי' שאין יכול לכפור באותו מנה הלכך כאלו יש לו שטר על אותו מנה ושעבוד קרקעות הוי וכו' עכ"ל: ויש להבין איך הביא דברי ירושלמי דסותר להדיא דברי הגמרא בב"מ דאותו סלע שלישי שהודה בו הלוה לא הוי ש"ק וכן מבואר בגמרא שתי' ה"ל ש"ק אבל באומר שלש לא הוי ש"ק כלל ועוד ק' הא משנה איירי בין במקום שכותבין ובין במקום שאין כותבין כמבואר בגמ' שם דף י"ו ע"ב דאוקמא ר"א למשנה במקום שכותבין ודייק מיני' דכותבין שובר וא"כ דבמקום שכותבין ואין כתובה בידה א"כ הא ס"ל להרא"ש כהרי"ף דבזה לא אמר ר"י הטוען אחר מעשה ב"ד ונאמן לומר פרעתי ויכול לכפור אבל לפי מש"ל הכל נכון דברייתא האמור בגמרא דידן כך הוא דנכתב בשטר סתם סלעין א"כ מעולם לא נעשה על סלע השלישי שטר דסתם סלעים שתי' א"כ אם הלוה מודה בג' ה"ל הודאת בע"פ ומה ש"ק יש כאן אבל בירושלמי כ' סלעין ונמחק א"כ אם מתחילה היה כותב שלשה היה השטר על הג' כמו על הב' וה"ל ש"ק רק עכשיו נמחק והלוה מודה בו הרי הודאה בש"ק ואי דלא יאמינו לו מה בכך מ"מ ש"ק מיקרי והיינו כמש"ל שטר שנאבד או אינו מקוים ולכן במקום שכותבין כתובה דהיה מתחילה ש"ק דהי' כתובה בידה אף דעכשיו א"א לטרוף משעבדי דיטענו פרוע מ"מ הוי ש"ק והא דכתב הירושלמי דלא יכול לכפור כמ"ש כ"ע מודים וכו' משום דמשנה איירי בכל גווני אפי' במקום שאין כותבין ושם אלו יכול לכפור מעול' לא חל ש"ק דלא כתבו כלל ופרעתי יכול לטעון והוי כמו מלוה ע"פ לדידן דבטלו לש"ד ולכך צ"ל דלא יכול לכפור וכו' אבל במקום שכותבין כיון דמתחילה היה שעבור לא נ"מ במה דיכול לכפור. ודברי הרא"ש ברורים והא דפי' הרא"ש כן בירושלמי דסלע ג' ה"ל שעבוד קרקע ולא פי' דברי חכמים כמ"ש בגמרא דידן דשנים הוי ש"ק וא"כ אלו אמר לוה שתים לא הוי שבועה דלא הוי ממין טענה דשנים ה"ל הודאה בקרקעות וא"כ אף באומר שלשה פטור דה"ל משיב אבידה דל"ל אערומי קמערי' דהא בשנים פטור משבועה וכ"כ הרא"ה דס"ל להרא"ש דזה אינו דהא ה"ל מגו דמ"מ לכופר בכל דבשנים א"א לכפור וצ"ל דבמקום דמסייע שטרא מעיז ולכך אמרינן דה"ל משיב אבידה בפ"ק דב"מ כמ"ש התו' להדיא וזהו בשטר שכתב בו סתם סלעין מסייע ליה שטר דלא היה יותר מב' סלעים דאלו היה יותר היו עדים כותבין משא"כ בברייתא דירושלמי דהיה כתוב ונמחק א"כ אין כאן סיוע משטר ואין זה משיב אבידה דה"ל מגו דמ"מ לכופר בכל דשנים צריך להודות ולכך פי' דהסלע ג' ה"ל כקרקע וא"ש ודוק. ומזו ירושלמי הוכיח הרא"ש דינו דאם תחילה היה ש"ק אף דנאבד מ"מ ש"ק מיקרי. ויש להקשות לפי שיטה זו מה פריך בגמרא למ"ד הילך פטור למה אצטריך קרא למעט קרקע משבועה הא אצטריך בכה"ג במ"מ ומכר קרקע לשיטת התו' והרא"ש אף דלא יאמינו לו הלקוחות מ"מ ש"ק מיקרי הואיל ובאמת נשתעבד לו קרקע אבל ודאי הילך לא מיקרי דהא א"י לטרוף כמלא מחט קרקע מלקוחות דלא יאמינו לו. דאף דכתבו התו' הא דאמרי' למה איצטרך קרא למעט קרקע אין הקושיא על התורה דאיצטרך קרא למילתא אחריני רק הקושי' על המשנה דלא ה"ל להביאו ובזמן המשנה כבר בטלו לשעבוד במלוה ע"פ ולק"מ. מ"מ ק' הא במלוה בשטר ואבד השטר דעת הרא"ש ותו' דה"ל ש"ק במודה ביה והילך ליכא דיוכל לכפור וגם אין גובה משעבדי דלא יאמינו לו וא"כ משום כך תני ליה במשנה. וצ"ל דזה ודאי דשטר ה"ל ש"ק הוא לכ"ע אפי' למ"ד של"ד דזה כללא בש"ס דשטר ה"ל ש"ק ולא יפול בו מחלוקת אי ש"ד דמה בכך דשל"ד השתא תקנו חכז"ל שישתעבדו נכסים והרי הן משועבדים לו וה"ל ש"ק אך זהו אם השטר לפנינו אבל באין השטר לפנינו רק הלוה מודה בו למ"ד שעבודא ל"ד הא אין כאן שיעבוד וחכמים דתקנו השעבוד היינו ביש לו שטר אבל בנאבד השטר בטל שעבודא של חכמים מעיקרא דהן אמרו שיגבה מלקוחות בישנו שטר בידו והן אמרו דלא יתקיים שעבודו באין השטר בידו ולא אמרו הרא"ש וסייעתו אלא למ"ד ש"ד רק במלוה ע"פ הפקיעו חז"ל ובשטר הניחו אותו על ד"ת אבל למ"ד של"ד לא וא"כ הקו' הגמרא למ"ד לאו דאורייתא דבזה לא יחלקו אי הילך חייב או פטור ומשמע להדיא בשמעתין דהמחליף דרב ושמואל ס"ל הילך פטור והן ס"ל של"ד וא"ש דל"ל בשטר דאם שטר קיים ה"ל הילד ובנאבד גם ש"ק לא מיקרי ובזו יש ליישב מש"ל ר"ס ע"ה דהקשו תו' ממינתא דר"י דשבועות ולא הקשו מיניה וביה דמה הבדל יש בין סלע שני לסלע הג' דאיכא למימר דהך תנא ס"ל של"ד כמש"ל סי' ל"ט דר"מ ס"ל כן ולכך פריך ממילתא דר"י דס"ל ש"ד ופשוט אך זהו דוחק כמש"ל:

אם אינו יכול לקיימו המחבר סתם בדין כרמב"ן וכפי שכתבתי בס"ק הקודם התו' והרא"ש חולקים דמ"מ היה שעבוד קרקעות ולא נ"מ במה דלא יאמינו לו הלקיחות וכן מצאתי באס"ז לב"מ שהביא בשם גדול א' דמפרש בהא דקאמרינן והא שטרא דקא מודה ביה הילך הוא דמיירי בשטר בלתי מקוים ולכך צריך להודאתו וצ"ל פי' לדבריו דלא תקשה מנ"ל לגמרא לפרש הברייתא בשטר בלתי מקוים דס"ל לגמרא דבר שא"א לכפור אין בכלל הודאה כלל וא"כ איך אמר ר"מ על האומר ג' משיב אבידה הרי זה מגו דמ"מ לכופר הכל דמה שהיה מודה בשתים אין בגדר הודאה כלל ולכך מוקי ליה הגמרא בשטר בלתי מקוים וא"כ שפיר הוי משיב אבידה דאף שנים בגדר הודאה דהרי יכול לכפור ולומר שטר מזויף ולכך פריך הגמרא שני' גופי' למה ישטור משבועה ואי דהיה טוען מזויף הא ה"ל מגו דמ"מ לכופר בכל אלא ע"כ כיון דמודה בי' ה"ל הילך ודחי' הגמרא דלכך פטור או דמסייע לי' שטרא או דה"ל ש"ק אף דהיה יכול לטעון מזויף מ"מ השתא דמודה ה"ל ש"ק. וכמ"ש התו' והרא"ש וארווח לן בהך מה שתמהו כולם דקארי ליה מה קארי ליה וכי לא ידע דאין נשבעין על כפירת שעבוד קרקעות ולפי דבריהם ניחא דס"ל הואיל השטר בלתי מקוים ונתקיי' עפ"י הלוה לא הוי שעבוד קרקעות כדעת הרמב"ן באמת ולכך משני הגמ' באמת דמ"מ הוי שעבוד קרקע כדעת התו' והרא"ש וגם מרוויחנא מה דקשה לס"ד דלא ידע מהך דה"ל ש"ק רק מטעם הילך ס"ל פטור בשתים א"כ אדמסייע מברייתא לסייע ממשנה דבריש פ"ב דכתובות כקושית הרא"ש דה"ל לבעל לישבע ש"ד דמ"מ וע"כ מטעם הילך פטור גם בהך תי' דמסייע לי' שטרא ולא מטעם הילך ולא מטעם ש"ק קשה הך משנה דכתובות מא"ל דשם לא שייך מסייע שטרא דכתובה אין בידה לדעת אי מנה או מאתים אך לפי הנ"ל דבמקוים ידע הך דה"ל שעבוד קרקעות ושם מקוים דאשה יש לה כתובה בתנאי ומעשה ב"ד לק"מ רק כאן ס"ל דאיירי בלתי מקוים כמ"ש כי לא ידע עדיין מסברת מסייע שטרא ואנן דפסקינן אפי' במקוים משי' אבידה משום דחדית לן גמרא סברא מסיי' שטרא ובכל אופן הוי משיב אבידה כמ"ש התו' ושפיר דייק וא"ש וא"כ הגאון הנ"ל נמי ס"ל כמ"ש התו' והרא"ש. ואולי אפשר אותו גאון ס"ל כדעת התו' בפ' א"נ דאם לוה אינו טוען מזויף לא טענינן ללקוחות מזויף ולא חיישי' לקנוניא וא"כ שפיר הוי ש"ק אבל לפי דעת הרמב"ן וכמש"ל בסי' ק"ו מזה באריכות דמ"מ טענינן להו מזויף א"כ תו ליכא שעבוד קרקעות. אך זהו דוחק דבהך דינא יחלקו המקשן ותרצן.

מיהו יהי' איך שיהיה עכ"פ דעת התו' ורא"ש חולקים אך אני תמה איך הביא הטור דברי תו' ורא"ש להלכה הא כתב הרא"ש בריש פ"ב דכתובות שהבאתי לעיל דלכך אין הבעל נשבע דה"ל הודה שעבוד קרקע וכתב דאף עכשיו תקנו שיהיה האשה גובה ממטלטלין מ"מ כיון דהטוען אחר מעשה ב"ד ל"א כלום ה"ל הילך דא"י לכפור וכו' הרי חדית לן הרא"ש לבתר תקנת הגאונים תו לא מיקרי שטר ש"ק רק מפטר בשבועה מתור' הילך ולפ"ז בשטר שנאבד דיכול לכפור תו לא הוי ש"ק וגם הילך לא שייך דהרי יכול לכפור וכ"כ המ"מ בהל' אישות פי"ז דפסק הרמב"ם בהיא אומרת בתולה הייתי והוא אומר אלמנה דישבע הבעל שבועה של תורה כדין מ"מ ותמה הראב"ד דה"ל שעבוד קרקעות וכתב המ"מ דס"ל לרמב"ם בתר תקנת גאונים ליטול ממטלטלין תו ליכא ש"ק וכתב מיהו מ"מ אינו יכול לכפור דהטוען אחר מעשה ב"ד וכו' והעלה דבמקום שכותבין כתוב' ואבדה דנאמן לומר פרעתי הרי יכול לכפור ואיכא תקנת גאונים לגבות מטלטלין חייב ש"ד ע"ש הרי דס"ל להדיא לולי תקנת הגאונים אף דיכול לטעון פרעתי מ"מ ה"ל שעבוד קרקעות והיינו כמ"ש להרא"ש ותו' מ"מ לבתר תקנת גאונים תו לא הוי ש"ק וא"כ לפ"ז לדידן נפל הך דינא דהיה שטר ונאבד בבירא דתו ליכא שעבוד קרקעות דהא גובין ממטלטלין לבתר תקנת גאונים. ואמת דהטור בא"ע סי' צ"ו הביא דעת הרא"ש בהך הוא אומר אלמנה והיא אומרת בתולה הייתי דבכ"מ אפילו במקום דכותבין כתובה אין נשבע רק היסת אף דשם נאמן לומר פרעתי ולא שייך הטוען אחר מעשה ב"ד רק כבר ישבו האחרונים וכתבו דהטור מיירי באופן דהיה מתרה אל תפרעני אלא בעדים דתו לא מצי לכפור אפילו במקום שכותבין אך כאן קשה. ודוחק לומר דבלאו הכי הקשה הרב לחם משנה מה בכך דתקנו גאונים לגבות מטלטלין הא שאר בעל חוב תמיד מדינא דגמרא גובה מטלטלין ומכל מקום אמרו דשטר מיקרי שעבוד קרקעות וצ"ל דודאי אף דמדינא זובה מטלטלין מ"מ שעבודא דאורייתא ליכא על מטלטלין רק מדרבנן אמרו לגבות מטלטלין ולירד לנכסיו אבל מהתורה אין גובין רק קרקע וכמ"ש המפורשים ולכך שטר מיקרי שעבוד קרקעות אף דגם גובה מטלטלין עיקר שעבודו על קרקעות. אך בכתובה כיון דגאונים תקנו ולדעת הרא"ש יש להם שרש ועיקר מדינא דגמרא גמלי דערבי אשה גובה כתובתה א"כ לא ה"ל שעבוד מקרקע ואי דעיקר שעבוד תורה בקרקעות ה"מ בשאר ב"ח אבל גופו של כתובה דרבנן הן אמרו והן אמרו ומה אילמא זה מזה ולכך לא איקרי שעבוד קרקע אך זהו דחוק. ובגוף הקושי' של הלח"מ נראה דהא דב"ח גובה ממטלטלין לאו דאינהו משעבדי דא"כ אף מיתמי נגבה כמו אלו עשה שורו אפותיקי דשיעבד מטלטלין בפי' גובה מיתמי כמ"ש הרשב"א רק צ"ל דלא משתעבדי כלל רק מיני' אפי' מגלימא וכו' מכח פריעת ב"ח מצוה אבל יתומים אין מחויבים בכך וא"כ דאינו בכלל השעבוד אף הוא בתובע שטרו אין תובע רק קרקע ולא מטלטלין דאין כלל שעבודו עליהם ולא ה"ל כתבעו קרקעות וכלים. משא"כ לתקנת הגאונים דתקנו לגבות אף מטלטלין דיתמי ש"מ דתקנו לשעבוד גמור כאלו כתב לב"ח מטלטלין בלי אגב דמשתעבד וגובה מיתמי ולא מלקוח' דל"ל קלא כמ"ש רשב"א וא"כ דנכנס בתוך השעבוד כמו קרקע ובתביעתו ה"ל כתבעו קרקע וכלים וא"ש ולכן גוף הקו' במ"ע ולכן נראה דבלא"ה כבר כתבנו כי אחרונים עמדו במ"ש הטור סתם דאפי' במקום דכותבין כתובה ואינה בידה אין על הבעל רק היסת דהא יכול לכפור ומ"ש דמיירי דהתרה אל תפרעני דוחק כנראה שם ולכך י"ל דקשיא לטור קו' הלח"מ מנ"מ בתקנות הגאונים כל ב"ח גובי' ממטלטלין כמש"ל ומ"ש לחלק לא שמיע ליה ולכך ס"ל בהרא"ש כך הפי' דמפרש על המשנה דקתני אם יש עדים הא ליכא עדים בעל מהימן ול"א דבעי שבועה משום דה"ל ש"ק ול"ק איך סתם וקתני תינח ביש לו קרקע באין לו קרקע מא"ל ה"ל למימר דישבע הבעל דז"א דבממ"נ אי ל"ל קרקע אין גובה כתובה כלל דאין כתובה נגבית רק מקרקע ואי א"ל קרקע הדר ה"ל ש"ק רק ק' תינח בגמרא אבל ברי"ף ק' איך העתיק סתם דבעל מהימן הא בדלית ליה קרקע א"נ בלי שבועה ואי דאינו במציאות הא הגאונים תקנו דגובה מטלטלין ולזה קאמר דמ"מ א"י לכפור או דהרא"ש דינא ביקש להודיענו דאפילו ל"ל קרקע לא משתבע וזהו כוונתו אפילו לתקנת הגאונים וכו' וא"כ הא יש במציאות דל"ל קרקע מ"מ אין כאן שבועה דלא יכול לכפור וכו' וזהו הכל בדל"ל קרקע אבל ביש לו קרקע אין מועיל במה דגבי' אף מן מטלטלין וש"ק לא זז ולכך הטור דמיירי בסתמא דא"ל קרקע כמ"ש כאן בשטר דהוי ש"ק ומיירי נמי דא"ל קרקע כמ"ש בס"ק הקודם וכמ"ש הש"ך א"כ אף שם בא"ע מיירי בסתמא דא"ל קרקע וא"כ לעולם הוי ש"ק אף דיכול לכפור כדעת התו' והרא"ש בסי' זה ול"מ מה שתוכל לגבות ממטלטלין ולכך כ' דאין לבעל רק שבועת היסת וכ"כ ברמזים באבדה כתובה והיינו במקום שכותבים אין לבעל רק היסת ולא כתב דלאחר התקנה ל"ש דין זה:

ועוד נראה יותר ברור ונכון לפמ"ש לקמן סי' ק"ז בישוב דברי הטור והרא"ש דסותרים זה את זה דפעם א' כתבו דתקנ' הגאונים לא מכח תקנה רק מדינא כמש"ל דה"ל כגמלי דערבי ופ"א כתבו דמ"מ לא הוה מדינא רקן מכח תקנה וע"ש שכתבתי דבנזיקין וכדומה דלא ה"ל לאתנוי' ולכתוב אמרי' דהוא מדינא אבל במקום דכותבין שטר ל"ל דהיו סומכין דעת' אמטלטלי דא"כ ה"ל לכתוב מטלטלין וקרקע ע"ש מ"ש באריכות ולפ"ז י"ל דס"ל להרא"ש אי מדינא סומכין דעתם על מטלטלין ומדינא גביה תו לא מקרי שטר ש"ק דגם מטלטלי הם משועבדים וה"ל כתבעו כלים וקרקעות והודה לו במקצת כלים וקרקעות דיש כאן ש"ד אבל אי מדינא לא גביה ולא סמכה דעת' כלל על המטלטלים רק מכח תקנה גביה תו לא פקע שיעבוד שטר מש"ק וא"כ דברי הרא"ש א"ש דהא דכ' הרא"ש אע"ג דבתר הגאונים אשה גובה ממטלטלי ל"א על מקום שכותבין דשם ס"ל למכתב וא"כ לא גביה מדינא רק קושיתו במקום דאין כותבין וה"ל ממש כגמלא דערבי והוי שיעבוד מטלטלין וע"ז דייק וע"ז שפיר משני בממ"נ דכל הספק הוא במקום שאין כותבין ואז הא אר"י הטוען אמב"ד וכו' והרי א"י לכפור וא"כ א"ש ודברי הרא"ש בכ"מ אמורי' הן במקום שכותבין דבלא"ה ל"מ תקנו' הגאונים כמ"ש והן במקום שא"כ דה"ל א"י לכפור ולכך סתם הטור הן ברמזים והן בטור דלעולם אין כאן ש"ד בממ"נ כמ"ש ולק"מ ומעתה יפה עשה הטור שבסי' זה לא הזכיר דבתר תקנות גאונים בנאבד השטר דיכול לכפור תו לא הוי ש"ק דבמקום שכותבין כמו שט"ח לא שייך הך דאין גובה ממטלטלי' דיתמי רק מכח תקנה ולא מדינא כמ"ש הטור בסי' ק"ז ולכך בלא"ה מש"ל במ"מ גרידא לא הוי ש"ק אפילו דנפרש כמ"ש הסמ"ע וש"ך דדעת התו' ורא"ש אפילו לדידן הוי מודה במקצת ש"ק אם אית ליה קרקע דזהו לא נכתב והדר ה"ל תקנת הגאונים דינא וליכא ש"ק ודוק. אך זהו דעת הטור והרא"ש אבל המ"מ דעתו ברמב"ם דאף במקום שכותבין כיון דנאבד השטר הרי יכול לכפור וש"ק ליכא לבתר תקנת הגאונים. והש"ע הביא שם בא"ע סי' צ"ו ב' דעות דעת הרמב"ם ודעת הרא"ש וכאן סתם כדעת הרמב"ם והרי זה סתם ואח"כ מחלוקת: וגם נ"ל מהנ"ל בהא דאמרינן בלי' ליה קרקע אף שטר לא מיקרי ש"ק אם יש לו קרקע שקנה אח"כ ובתוך השטר לא שיעבד ליה דתקני אם אמרינן דהוי ש"ק או לא דהא לא משתעבד ליה ונראה דתלי במחלוקת להרמב"ן דאם מת הלוה אין גובה מיתומים כלל רק מיני' א"כ אין כאן שעבוד כלל וה"ל כמטלטלין לדינא דגמרא בכל ב"ח דמ"מ לא נכנסו בכלל כשעבוד דנימא דה"ל כתבעו קרקע ומטלטלין אבל להחולקים דאף מיורש גובה א"כ הרי זה כמו מטלטלין לבתר תקנת גאונים אף דאם מכרן אין לב"ח הימנו וה"ל ש"ק:
en_segments: That a promissory note is treated like land. The Sema holds, as he explains at length in the Derishah, that even if the debtor never had land and presently has none, a debt evidenced by a promissory note is nevertheless considered a claim secured by land merely because a lien on land is mentioned in the note. The Taz follows him. Their proof is from the Tur, who cites Tosafot and the Rosh as saying that according to the view that a lien on property is of Torah origin, one cannot find a Torah oath in a case of partial admission and the like except where the debtor has no land. They infer that a note must be treated as a land secured obligation even where the debtor has no land. If the debtor actually had land, then even an oral loan or a handwritten acknowledgment would also be secured by land. The distinction must therefore be that a formal promissory note itself is treated as a land secured claim even where there is no land. The Shach disagrees, and the Bach appears to agree with him. In their view, if the debtor has no land, even a promissory note has no land lien and cannot be called a land secured claim. The reason a promissory note is sometimes called a land secured obligation, while an oral loan and handwritten acknowledgment are not, is that the creditor may waive his right against the debtor personally without waiving his right against encumbered property. It is for that reason that the formal note is described as secured by land. It is true that Tosafot at the beginning of Bava Metzia, in the sugya of heilech, write a distinction of this kind. Yet it is difficult to fit into the Tur's language. The Tur should not have stated without qualification that a promissory note is a land secured obligation. He should have specified the circumstances described by the Shach, where the creditor waived recourse against the debtor personally but not against encumbered property. There is another difficulty. The Tur first cites Ramban's position that if the note was lost or cannot be authenticated, it is not considered a land secured claim. The Tur then writes: but Tosafot and the Rosh say that partial admission requiring a Torah oath can be found only where the debtor has no land, etc. This clearly indicates that Tosafot and the Rosh disagree with Ramban. According to the Shach, however, Ramban could fully agree with their statement. Ramban may simply be speaking about the kind of note described by the Shach, where the creditor waived recourse against the debtor personally but retained recourse against encumbered property. So long as the note exists and is enforceable, he can collect from purchasers and it is therefore a land secured claim. If the note is lost or cannot be authenticated, he can no longer collect from purchasers and it is no longer a land secured claim. There would be no dispute at all. It therefore appears that the Derishah was troubled by Tosafot in Shevuot. Regarding Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one who denies a loan supported by witnesses is liable for a false oath offering, whereas one who denies a loan evidenced by a promissory note is exempt because it is a claim secured by land, Tosafot and the Rosh ask that Rabbi Yochanan holds that liens are of Torah origin. If so, even a loan supported by witnesses should be a claim secured by land. Tosafot answer that the debtor has no land, or that the creditor waived the land lien. The question still remains: if the debtor has no land, then the loan evidenced by a promissory note should likewise not be land secured. Tosafot in Bava Metzia themselves notice this and answer, as the Shach does, that the creditor may have waived recourse against the debtor personally without waiving recourse against encumbered property. But in Shevuot they do not raise or answer this second question. Maharam of Lublin already expresses astonishment at this in his novellae to Bava Metzia. The Derishah sought to prove from the omission that Tosafot there hold that even without existing land, a formal promissory note itself is considered land secured. In truth, the Shach is correct that such a proposition has no sound basis. The difficulty in Tosafot and the Rosh can be resolved easily. They may hold, like most authorities, that after the Sages enacted that an oral loan cannot be collected from purchasers, there is no operative lien at all upon the borrower's land as against purchasers. At every moment the borrower may sell his land without the creditor being able to prevent it. The fact that the creditor can collect from land that remains in the borrower's possession does not reflect a continuing property lien. It is merely the general rule that collection from the debtor himself may be made even from the cloak on his back. Thus an oral loan no longer has the status of a land secured obligation. Tosafot's question there, however, concerns the Torah's original law. The Torah imposes an oath in a case of partial admission. According to the view that liens are of Torah origin, an ordinary debt under Torah law would be secured by land. Where, then, is the Torah oath of partial admission found? Tosafot answer that under the Torah law one finds such an oath where the debtor has no land or where the creditor waived the land lien. Rabbi Yochanan's statement, by contrast, concerns practical halachah after the Sages enacted that an oral loan does not collect from purchasers and thereby removed its land lien. Therefore, even where the debtor owns land, one who falsely denies an oral loan supported by witnesses can be liable for the oath offering because the debt is no longer treated as a land secured claim. A formal promissory note is different. Its lien against purchasers remains in force because the Sages did not remove it. Everything is thus properly explained. This, in my view, is clearly the Tur's understanding. For this reason, throughout siman 75 and siman 87, where the Tur discusses the rules of Torah oaths and the distinctions between Torah and rabbinic oaths, he never states that the borrower must specifically be a person who owns no land or that the creditor must have waived the lien. As practical halachah, no such condition exists. Even where the borrower owns land, the Sages removed the purchaser lien from an oral loan. This applies to an oral loan or handwritten acknowledgment. A formal promissory note, however, retains its land lien when the debtor has land. This is the actual distinction between a formal note and an oral or handwritten debt. The Tur cites Tosafot and the Rosh to establish precisely this conceptual point. The Ran in Shevuot, whose words I discussed at length above in siman 75, answers the original difficulty differently. What does it matter that the debtor's property is legally subject to the debt? If the creditor later seeks to collect from purchasers, the purchasers will deny the debtor's admission and say, "What does your admission matter to us? You are speaking falsely. You never borrowed, or you already paid." Accordingly, the admitted portion is not practically collectible from purchasers and should not be considered an admission concerning land, even if the Torah recognizes a general land lien. Ramban too accepts this answer, as the Rosh cites in his name at the end of chapter Shevuat HaPikadon. Tosafot and especially the Rosh there reject this answer. They hold that once the underlying obligation is one for which land is legally encumbered, it is treated as a land secured claim even if, in practice, the creditor cannot collect from purchasers because they will not accept the debtor's admission. Therefore, under Torah law, an ordinary loan secured by land does not generate a Torah oath of partial admission, and we must establish the Torah's oath in a case where the debtor has no land. The practical difference between these approaches emerges with a formal promissory note whose purchaser lien normally remains intact but which has been lost, while the debtor admits that it existed. According to Ramban, the debt is no longer a land secured claim because the creditor cannot collect from purchasers. They are entitled to reject the debtor's admission and say that perhaps there never was a note or perhaps the debt was repaid. The debtor's partial admission can therefore generate a Torah oath. According to Tosafot and the Rosh, however, the underlying debt is of a type that carried a land lien from its inception. The inability to collect from purchasers because the note was lost does not change the nature of the debt. This is exactly like the Torah law of partial admission discussed above, where the purchaser may not practically believe the debtor but the claim is still characterized as land secured because of the underlying lien. Thus, even when the note has been lost or cannot be authenticated, if the debtor admits its existence, no Torah oath of partial admission arises. This is clear and correct. See the Rosh at the end of chapter Shevuat HaPikadon and his words will explicitly support this explanation. The same is evident in chapter 2 of Ketubot. The Rosh discusses a husband who says, "I married you as a widow and your ketubah is one hundred," while the woman says, "I was a virgin and my ketubah is two hundred." He explains that the husband does not take a Torah oath as one who partially admits because the ketubah is a land secured obligation. The Rosh cites the Yerushalmi concerning a note stating unspecified sela'im where part of the writing was erased. The creditor says the amount was five and the debtor says it was three. Ben Azzai says that since the debtor partially admits the claim he must swear. The Sages say that this is not an admission of the same kind as the claim. The Rosh explains that the admission concerns land. Although the remaining text of the note itself proves only two sela'im, once the debtor admits a third, it is treated as though the third had also been written into the note. The denial concerns movable money while the admission concerns a land secured debt. The Yerushalmi then asks from the ketubah case. There, seemingly, the husband's admission is of the same kind as the woman's claim. She no longer holds a note in her hand. She says two hundred and he says one hundred. The Yerushalmi answers that everyone agrees she is entitled to one hundred, meaning that he cannot deny that basic amount. Therefore, it is treated as though she has a note for that one hundred, and that portion is land secured. At first glance this passage is very difficult. How can the Rosh cite the Yerushalmi when it appears to contradict the Bavli in Bava Metzia? In the Bavli's case of a note saying merely "sela'im," where the debtor admits three, the third sela is not treated as a land secured obligation. The Gemara explicitly distinguishes the first two sela'im, which are evidenced by the note, from the third, which exists only by the debtor's oral admission. There is another difficulty. The Mishnah concerning the ketubah applies both in a place where ketubot are ordinarily written and in a place where they are not, as is clear from Ketubot 16b, where Rabbi Elazar establishes the Mishnah in a place where ketubot are written and derives from it that a receipt may be written. In a place where ketubot are written, if the woman does not present her ketubah, the Rosh follows the Rif that Rabbi Yochanan's rule that one cannot plead payment against an obligation imposed by beit din does not apply. The husband can claim that he paid. How then can the Yerushalmi say that he cannot deny the first one hundred and that it is treated as though a note exists? According to what I have written, everything is correct. The baraita cited in the Bavli concerns a note that originally stated only the unspecified word "sela'im." An unspecified plural means two. No formal note ever existed for the third sela. Thus, when the debtor admits a third, that third amount is only an oral admission. There never was a land lien evidenced by the note for it. The Yerushalmi, however, speaks of a note that contained an amount which was later erased. If the note originally stated three, then the third sela was originally secured by the written note exactly like the first two. The fact that the writing is now erased and purchasers will not accept the debtor's admission does not matter according to the Rosh's view. The underlying third sela was originally a land secured debt. It is therefore treated as an admission concerning land, just as I explained above regarding a lost or unauthenticated note. The same applies to the ketubah in a place where ketubot are ordinarily written. Originally, when the ketubah existed, the basic one hundred was land secured. Even though the woman now cannot collect from purchasers because she lacks the document and they may claim it was paid, the underlying obligation was originally secured. According to the Rosh, that is sufficient to characterize the husband's admission as concerning land. Why then does the Yerushalmi emphasize that the husband cannot deny the basic one hundred? Because the Mishnah also applies in a place where no ketubah document is ordinarily written. In such a place, if the husband could plead payment, there may never have been any written instrument or enduring land lien at all. The obligation could resemble an oral debt whose purchaser lien was removed. Therefore the Yerushalmi explains that everyone agrees the woman is entitled to the basic one hundred. In a place where no writing is customary, the obligation created by beit din itself gives her an unavoidable basic claim. But in a place where ketubot are written, once the obligation was originally secured, it makes no difference that he may now plead payment. The Rosh's words are thus entirely clear. The Rosh does not explain the Sages in the Yerushalmi the way the Bavli explains its own baraita, namely that the first two sela'im are a land secured admission and therefore, had the debtor merely admitted two, there would be no oath, while an admission of three still leaves him as one who voluntarily returns a lost item because he could have admitted only the two already stated in the note. The Raah explains along those lines. The Rosh does not, because in the Yerushalmi case the note originally contained more and was later erased. There is no written support for the proposition that only two were owed. Thus the debtor is not like one voluntarily returning a lost item by admitting the third. In the Bavli's case, by contrast, the note itself says merely "sela'im," which ordinarily means two. That writing supports the debtor's claim that no more than two were owed. He could therefore be viewed as voluntarily admitting the third, and Tosafot explicitly use the fact that the note supports him to explain why he is considered one returning a lost item even though ordinarily one who partially admits has a migo to deny everything. The note's text gives him unusual boldness to deny beyond the two because it supports his position. In the Yerushalmi, where the original amount was written and later erased, there is no such support from the document. The debtor cannot be considered one returning a lost item merely because he admits three. The Rosh therefore explains the Sages' exemption by saying that the third sela itself is treated as a land secured admission. Everything fits precisely. From this Yerushalmi the Rosh could indeed derive his rule that where a debt was originally secured by a note, the loss or erasure of the note does not remove its characterization as a land secured obligation for purposes of a Torah oath. One may ask according to this approach from the Gemara's question against the opinion that heilech exempts: why did Scripture need a special exclusion to exempt land from an oath? Even if heilech generally exempts, the exclusion for land should still be necessary in a case of partial admission where land was originally encumbered but later sold, according to Tosafot and the Rosh. Purchasers will not accept the debtor's admission, so the creditor cannot actually collect even a needle's worth of land from them. The admission would therefore not be heilech. Yet according to the Rosh it remains a land secured admission because the original lien existed. Tosafot themselves explain that when the Gemara asks why a verse is needed to exclude land, the question is not literally whether the Torah could have used the verse for some other law. The question is why the Mishnah needed to teach the land exclusion as an independent application. By the era of the Mishnah, the Sages had already removed the purchaser lien from oral loans. Thus the ordinary cases before the Mishnah would not involve a surviving land lien on an oral partial admission. This removes much of the difficulty. Still, one can ask from a formal promissory note that was later lost. According to the Rosh and Tosafot, if the debtor admits the debt it remains a land secured claim, but because the note is lost the creditor cannot collect from purchasers who reject the admission. It is therefore not heilech. Why then was the Mishnah's exclusion of land not needed for precisely such a case? We must say that the proposition that a formal note is a land secured claim is itself accepted even according to the opinion that liens are not of Torah origin. The Gemara routinely treats a formal promissory note as land secured without making that characterization depend upon the Torah origin of liens. Even if liens are not of Torah origin, the Sages established a purchaser lien for formal notes, and actual land becomes legally subject to the debt. But this is so only when the note exists and is enforceable. If the note is no longer present and only the debtor admits that it once existed, according to the opinion that liens are not of Torah origin there is no original Torah lien to preserve. The rabbinic lien was enacted only so long as the creditor possesses the enforceable note. Once the note is lost, the very rabbinic framework that created the purchaser lien no longer applies. The Sages said that he may collect from purchasers when the note is in his hand, and they equally determined that the lien is not enforceable when it is not. The Rosh and those who agree with him say that a lost note remains a land secured claim only according to the view that liens are of Torah origin. Under that view, the underlying debt carried a Torah lien from the outset. Although the Sages removed the lien from oral loans, they left the Torah lien intact in the case of a formal promissory note. The loss of the document may prevent practical collection from purchasers, but it does not change the original Torah character of the debt. According to the view that liens are not of Torah origin, however, once the rabbinic purchaser lien becomes unenforceable because the note is absent, no land secured status remains. The Gemara's question concerning heilech can therefore be understood according to the opinion that liens are not of Torah origin. Indeed, the sugya concerning an exchange indicates that Rav and Shmuel hold that heilech exempts, and they also hold that liens are not of Torah origin. Under their view, there is no case of a lost note that simultaneously remains a land secured claim and yet fails to be heilech. If the note exists, the claim is land secured and collection can proceed against the encumbered property. If the note is lost, the rabbinic lien itself no longer gives the claim land secured status. The Gemara's question is therefore properly framed. This also provides one way to answer a point I raised above at the beginning of siman 75. Tosafot there ask from Rabbi Yochanan's statement in Shevuot rather than asking internally from the baraita itself why there should be any difference between the first two sela'im stated in the note and the third sela admitted orally. One may say that the baraita's tanna could hold that liens are not of Torah origin, as I wrote above in siman 39 regarding Rabbi Meir. The first two are nevertheless secured because they are in the formal note, while the third admitted orally is not. Tosafot therefore challenge from Rabbi Yochanan, who himself holds that liens are of Torah origin. This is straightforward, although, as I wrote above, the matter may still be somewhat strained.

If he cannot establish it, the Mechaber states the law without qualification in accordance with the Ramban. As I wrote in the preceding seif katan, Tosafot and the Rosh disagree, for in any event there was a lien upon land, and it makes no difference that the purchasers would not believe him. I likewise found in the Asufot Zekenim to Bava Metzia, in the name of one of the great authorities, an explanation of the statement, “But the document that he admits to is heilech,” as referring to an uncertified document, so that his admission is required. According to that authority, the explanation must be as follows. One might ask why the Gemara assumes that the baraita concerns an uncertified document. The Gemara holds that something which cannot be denied is not considered an admission at all. If so, how could Rabbi Meir say concerning one who says, “three,” that he is returning a lost object because he has a migo that he could have denied everything? His admission to two would not be an admission in the legal sense at all. Therefore the Gemara establishes the case as one of an uncertified document. Then he is indeed returning a lost object, because even the two are within the category of an admission, since he could have denied them by claiming that the document was forged. The Gemara then asks why, regarding the two themselves, he should be exempt from an oath. If the reason is that he could have claimed forgery, then he has a migo that he could have denied everything. Rather, once he admits to the document, it is heilech. The Gemara answers that he is exempt either because the document supports him or because it is a claim involving a lien on land. Even though he could have claimed forgery, now that he admits the document it is nevertheless a land lien, as Tosafot and the Rosh wrote. This also resolves the question raised by all the commentators, namely, what did the questioner initially think? Did he not know that one does not take an oath concerning denial of a land lien? According to this explanation, it is clear. The questioner thought that since the document was uncertified and was established only through the borrower’s own admission, it was not a land lien, which is in fact the view of the Ramban. The Gemara answers that it nevertheless is a land lien, in accordance with Tosafot and the Rosh. This also resolves another difficulty. According to the initial assumption, before the Gemara knew that it was a land lien and exempted the defendant only because of heilech, why did it seek support from the baraita rather than from the Mishnah at the beginning of the second chapter of Ketubot, as the Rosh asks? There too the husband should have been obligated to take a Torah oath as one who admits part of the claim, and necessarily he is exempt because of heilech. Likewise, according to the answer that the document supports him, without relying either on heilech or on a land lien, the Mishnah in Ketubot remains difficult. There the document cannot be said to support the husband, because the woman’s ketubah does not itself establish whether she is entitled to one hundred or two hundred. According to what was explained, however, there is no difficulty. With a certified document the Gemara already knew that there is a land lien, and there the obligation is certified because a woman has a ketubah by stipulation and by act of beit din. Only here did the Gemara initially assume that the case concerns an uncertified document, because it had not yet introduced the rationale that the document itself supports him. We, however, rule that even with a certified document he is considered one who returns a lost object, because the Gemara introduced the additional rationale that the document supports him, and in every form of the case he is therefore returning a lost object, as Tosafot wrote. The inference is thus sound. If so, the great authority cited above likewise follows the approach of Tosafot and the Rosh. Perhaps that authority held like Tosafot in the chapter Eizehu Neshekh, that where the borrower himself does not claim forgery, beit din does not make a forgery claim for the purchasers and we do not suspect collusion. In that case it is indeed a land lien. According to the Ramban, however, and as I explained at length below in siman 106, we nevertheless make the forgery claim on behalf of the purchasers. If so, there would no longer be any lien upon land. This is somewhat strained, however, because it would mean that the questioner and the answerer in the Gemara disagree on that separate rule. However , however the matter is understood, Tosafot and the Rosh certainly disagree with the Ramban. I am nevertheless surprised that the Tur cites the words of Tosafot and the Rosh as practical law. The Rosh wrote at the beginning of the second chapter of Ketubot, as cited above, that the husband does not swear because his admission concerns a lien upon land. He then wrote that even after the enactment that a woman may collect from movable property, since one who makes a claim contrary to an act of beit din accomplishes nothing, this is heilech because he cannot deny the obligation. The Rosh thus taught that after the enactment of the Geonim a document is no longer called a land lien, and the exemption from a Torah oath rests instead upon heilech. Accordingly, where a document was lost and the debtor can deny the obligation, there is neither a land lien nor heilech, since he can deny it. The Maggid Mishneh likewise writes in chapter 17 of Hilkhot Ishut concerning the Rambam’s ruling where she says, “I was a virgin,” and he says, “you were a widow,” that the husband must take a Torah oath as one who admits part of the claim. The Raavad objects that this is a lien upon land. The Maggid Mishneh explains that the Rambam holds that after the enactment of the Geonim permitting collection from movable property there is no longer a land lien. He adds, however, that ordinarily the husband still cannot deny the obligation because one who contests an act of beit din is not believed. He therefore concludes that in a place where ketubot are written, if the ketubah was lost and the husband is believed to say that he paid it, he can deny the obligation, and because the enactment of the Geonim allows collection from movable property he is obligated in a Torah oath. See there. It is explicit from his words that without the Geonic enactment, even though the husband could claim payment, it would nevertheless be a land lien. This is precisely what I wrote concerning the Rosh and Tosafot. Yet after the Geonic enactment it is no longer a land lien. If so, according to our law the ruling concerning a document that was lost has fallen away entirely, because nowadays movable property may be collected under the Geonic enactment. It is true that in Even HaEzer siman 96 the Tur cites the Rosh’s view concerning the case where he says that she was a widow and she says that she was a virgin, ruling that in every place, even where ketubot are written, the husband takes only a heset oath. There too he is believed to claim payment and the principle concerning one who contests an act of beit din does not apply. The later authorities have already addressed this and explained that the Tur is speaking of a case where the husband had warned her not to accept payment except before witnesses, so that he can no longer deny even in a place where ketubot are written. But here the difficulty remains. One might answer, though with difficulty, that the Lechem Mishneh already asked why the Geonic enactment should matter at all. Any ordinary creditor may collect movable property under Talmudic law, and nevertheless a debt evidenced by a document is called a land lien. We must say that although the creditor may collect movable property as a matter of Talmudic law, movable property is not subject to a Torah lien. The Sages merely empowered him to collect movable property and descend to the debtor’s assets, while by Torah law collection is only from land, as the commentators wrote. Therefore a document is called a land lien even though movable property may also be collected, because the essential lien rests upon land. A ketubah may be different. Since the Geonim enacted collection from movable property, and according to the Rosh the enactment has a root and basis in Talmudic law, such as the case of the camels of Arabia from which a woman collects her ketubah, the obligation is not exclusively a lien upon land. If one were to say that the primary Torah lien is nevertheless upon land, that applies to ordinary creditors. A ketubah itself is rabbinic, and the Sages who created it also defined its mode of collection. There would therefore be no stronger reason to characterize the land than the movable property as the principal lien. Still, this distinction is strained. Regarding the Lechem Mishneh’s underlying question, it seems that when an ordinary creditor collects movable property, it is not because the movable property itself is encumbered. If it were, he should also collect it from orphans, just as when a person expressly designates his ox as an apotiki, thereby expressly encumbering movable property, the creditor may collect it from the heirs, as the Rashba writes. Rather, movable property is not subject to the lien at all. The debtor himself is liable even from the garment upon his shoulders because repayment of a debt is a mitzvah, but the orphans are not personally obligated in that mitzvah. Consequently, movable property is not part of the lien. Even when the creditor presents his document, his secured claim is only against land, not against movable property, and it is not a claim that combines land and utensils. By contrast, under the enactment of the Geonim, which permits collection even from the movable property of orphans, it is clear that they instituted an actual lien, as though the debtor had written that movable property would be encumbered to the creditor without attaching it to land. Such movable property is encumbered and may be collected from heirs, although not from purchasers because it lacks publicity, as the Rashba writes. Once movable property enters the lien in the same manner as land, a claim upon the document becomes like a claim upon land and utensils together. The Lechem Mishneh’s difficulty is therefore resolved on its own. Nevertheless, it appears that even apart from this, the later authorities already noted a difficulty in the Tur’s unqualified ruling that even in a place where ketubot are written, if the ketubah is not in her possession, the husband takes only a heset oath. The explanation that the Tur is speaking of a case where he warned her not to accept payment except before witnesses is strained, as is evident there. It may therefore be that the Tur was troubled by the Lechem Mishneh’s question: what practical difference is created by the Geonic enactment if every creditor already collects movable property? He did not accept the distinction offered above. He therefore understood the Rosh differently. The Mishnah teaches that where witnesses exist the husband is believed, which implies that without witnesses he is believed without a Torah oath because the admission concerns a land lien. One might ask how the Mishnah can state the rule without qualification. Granted, where he owns land, but where he owns no land what can be said? There the husband should have to take an oath. The answer is that if he owns no land the ketubah cannot be collected at all, because originally a ketubah was collected only from land. If he does own land, it is again a land lien. The difficulty is only with the Rif, who reproduces the ruling without qualification that the husband is believed. After the Geonim enacted collection from movable property, there is now a practical case where the husband owns no land yet the ketubah may still be collected. The Rosh therefore explains that even then he cannot deny, because a claim contrary to an act of beit din is ineffective. Alternatively, the Rosh intended to teach an independent law, that even if the husband has no land he does not swear. This is the meaning of his statement that “even after the enactment of the Geonim” the result is unchanged. There now exists a case where he owns no land, yet there is still no oath because he cannot deny the obligation. Accordingly, all the words of the Rosh apply where the debtor has no land. Where he does have land, the fact that movable property may also be collected does not remove the status of the claim as a land lien. Therefore the Tur, who speaks in the ordinary case where the debtor has land, as I explained in the preceding seif katan and as the Shach also wrote, rules here that the document remains a land lien. So too in Even HaEzer the Tur speaks ordinarily of a husband who owns land. It therefore always remains a land lien even though collection is also possible from movable property. This is why the Tur rules that the husband is obligated only in a heset oath. Similarly, in his Kitzur Piskei HaRosh he writes that where a ketubah was lost, namely in a place where ketubot are written, the husband takes only a heset oath, and he does not say that the law changed after the enactment. This understanding resolves the difficulty. Furthermore , a clearer and more correct explanation follows from what I write below in siman 107 in resolving the apparent contradiction in the words of the Tur and the Rosh. In one place they write that the Geonic enactment was not merely an enactment but follows from the underlying law, as above, because movable property is like the camels of Arabia. Elsewhere they write that it is not the underlying law but only an enactment. There I explained that in damages and similar obligations, where the creditor had no opportunity to stipulate and write security terms, we say that collection from movable property is rooted in the law itself. But where a document is written, it cannot be said that the parties relied upon movable property. Had they intended that, the document should have expressly mentioned both movable property and land. See there at length. Accordingly, the Rosh may hold that where reliance upon movable property and collection from it exist by the underlying law, a document is no longer called a land lien, because movable property too is truly encumbered. The claim is then like one who claims utensils and land and the defendant admits part of both, which produces a Torah oath. But where movable property is not collectible by the underlying law, and the parties did not rely upon it, and collection exists only because of the enactment, the original lien evidenced by the document never loses its character as a land lien. The Rosh’s words are therefore precise. When he writes that even after the Geonim a woman collects from movable property, he is not speaking of a place where ketubot are written. In such a place the parties could have written the security expressly, and thus collection from movable property is not by the underlying law. His question concerns a place where ketubot are not written, where the case is truly comparable to the camels of Arabia and movable property is legally encumbered. In that setting he answers that the husband cannot deny the obligation, because Rabbi Yochanan said that one who contests an act of beit din accomplishes nothing. The Rosh’s rulings thus apply in all circumstances. In a place where ketubot are written, the Geonic enactment does not alter the character of the original lien. In a place where they are not written, the husband cannot deny the obligation. Therefore the Tur rules without qualification, both in his Kitzur Piskei HaRosh and in the Tur itself, that there is never a Torah oath, for one of these two reasons always applies. It follows that the Tur acted correctly in not stating here that after the Geonic enactment, where a document was lost and the debtor can deny the obligation, it ceases to be a land lien. With an ordinary written loan, the rule resembles a place where documents are written. Movable property of heirs is collected only because of the enactment, not under the underlying law, as the Tur himself writes in siman 107. Therefore the document remains a land lien. The same is true even if we adopt only the explanation of the Sema and the Shach that Tosafot and the Rosh hold that even nowadays an admission of part of a documented claim is a land lien where the debtor owns land. If this were not so, the Geonic enactment itself would determine the law and there would be no land lien. Examine this carefully. This, however, is the view of the Tur and the Rosh. The Maggid Mishneh understands the Rambam differently. According to him, even in a place where documents are written, once the document is lost and the debtor can deny the obligation, after the Geonic enactment there is no longer a land lien. The Shulchan Aruch in Even HaEzer siman 96 cites both opinions, the Rambam’s view and the Rosh’s view, whereas here the Mechaber rules without qualification like the Rambam. This is thus a case of an anonymous ruling followed elsewhere by a dispute. It also appears from the foregoing that where we say that if the debtor owns no land even a document is not considered a land lien, there is a question regarding land that he acquired later, where the document did not expressly include a clause encumbering property to be acquired in the future. Is that later acquired land enough to characterize the claim as a land lien? It seems that this depends upon a dispute. According to the Ramban, if the borrower dies the creditor cannot collect such property from the heirs at all, only from the borrower himself. If so, there is no true lien upon that property, and the case resembles movable property under the Talmudic rule governing ordinary creditors. Since the property never entered the lien, the claim cannot be treated as one upon both land and movable property. According to those who disagree with the Ramban and hold that even from heirs such later acquired property may be collected, it resembles movable property after the enactment of the Geonim. Although the creditor cannot collect it from purchasers, it nevertheless forms part of the lien, and the claim is therefore treated as one involving land.

he_segments: אפ"ה פטור וכו' ופי' הסמ"ע מש"ד אבל היסת חייב והב"ח השיג דאף מהיסת פטור והש"ך בס"ק נ"ג הסכים לסמ"ע וכ' שכ"כ הנ"י ואעפ"י שכתב הנ"י שהרשב"א והר"ן דחו ראית הרמב"ן מ"מ יוכל להיות דבדינ' ל"פ עליו וכן אפשר לפ' דעת הטור ולא הבנתי דבריו דבנ"י דהביא מחלוקת הרמב"ן והרשב"א לא ע"ז הביאו רק בדלעיל באומר שתי' אי צריך לישבע היסת או לא בזו נחלקו בראיה אבל זה כבר כ' הטור והמחבר לעיל באומר שתי' דחייב לישבע היסת וא"כ תמהני וביחוד על הב"ח כיון דהעלה הטור במודה רק בשתי' חייב היסת היאך ס"ד במודה בשלשה דפטור מהיסת א"כ אערומ' קמערים אי אמרי' שתי' אצטרך לישבע אמינא שלשה ואהי' פטור מכל וכל ופשיטא דאי בזה חייב היסת אף בזה חייב ושגגה יצא מלפני השליט הב"ח.

או לאביך וכו' הש"ך העתיק בס"ק נ"ה דברי ר"ה גאון ואני אעתיקו בקצרה שורש דבריו יורש שטען היה לאבי בידך ק' זוז והוא אומר אין לו בידי רק חמשי' פטור משבועה דה"ל משיב אבידה אבל אם אמר אמת היה לי מאה מאביך בידי ופרעתיו נו"ן חייב שבועה אם לא שקדמה הודאה לתביעה והוא שלא יהיה כמערים ואם יש עדים או קול שהיה מו"מ בינו לבין המת אף שקדמה הודאה מ"מ חייב עכ"ל בקיצור ודבריו תמוהים דאם פוסק כרבנן דפליגי אראב"י וס"ל בבנו מעיז א"כ אף באומר פרעתיו ה"ל משיב אבידה וכמו כן במ"ש דאם יש עדים וקול דאפילו בהודה קודם לתביעה צריך שבועה למה הא מ"מ משיב אבידה דאף דנימא כדעת הש"ך דעדים מעידים שהלוהו בבירור מ"מ הא הוא משיב אבידה דמצי לומר דפרע הכל דהא בבנו מעיז והש"ך ביקש לפ' דמיירי דיורש טוען ברי שהלוה לך אבי אבל א"י אם פרעת וזה מוסיף תימא יותר דא"כ אין היורש טוען ברי אם פרע או לא פרע וא"כ לכ"ע ליכא כאן שבועה דלא הוי טענת ברי ופשוט וגם ק' הא בגמרא מבואר דטוען פרעתיו כדאמר והאכלתיו פרס ומ"מ ס"ל לרבנן דכוותייהו פסק הגאון דה"ל משיב אבידה. והרב הש"ך חשב דר"ה גאון מפרש דפליגי בקדמה הודאה לתביעה אבל אח"כ חכמים מודים דחייב ש"ד ומלבד דאין זה מועיל דא"כ בקדמה התביעה אפילו באומר לא לויתי רק חמשים דלמא ס"ל לחכמים דחייב אף גם דקשה הך דבעינן התביעה קודם להודאה אין ענין כלל לפלוגתא גבי בנו ה"ל לומר כן בבע"ד עצמו אי בעינן תביעה קודם להודאה או לא. ומה ענין בנו מעיז לכך וזהו כללא הוא כמ"ש הרמב"ן בשם ר"ה גאון דבכ"מ בעינן תביעה קודם להודאה ואין זה ענין מחלוקתם כלל רק פליגי בקדמה תביעה כמ"ש הרמב"ן ולכך אין אני מוצא בכל
